statement: crate::code_graph::SymbolNode stores only a 1-based start line, no end line and no byte span. get_code_snippet (crates/enforcer-memory/src/snippet.rs) and search_code (crates/enforcer-memory/src/code_search.rs) both need a symbol's extent/containment, so both independently derive it the same way: a symbol's range runs from its start line up to (but not including) the next symbol's start line in the same file, or end-of-file if it is the last symbol -- a documented, deterministic convention, not a claim of exact AST extent.
why: The alternative (re-parsing with tree-sitter inside these modules to recover a real end-line) would duplicate crate::languages extraction logic and risk drifting from whatever crate::code_graph eventually does with real spans; the line-based convention is simple, byte-exact against the file on disk (satisfies the snippet hash-equality hard test), and consistent across both modules that need it.
howToApply: If crate::code_graph::SymbolNode ever gains a real end_line/end_byte field (X06.2 follow-up), both snippet.rs's line_range_to_byte_range and code_search.rs's containing_symbol/structural_score should switch to it -- the convention here is a documented placeholder, not a design endpoint.

statement: docs/plans/enforcer-selfhost-plan/refs/x06-baseline-tool-schemas.md (a coordinator-authored ground-truth extraction of the C baseline's exact wire behavior) landed on origin/rust-build partway through this lane's implementation pass, and its findings CORRECTED assumptions already baked into code written from the earlier, coarser scout digest: get_graph_schema must order labels/edge_types by descending row count (not alphabetical, as the scout digest's high-level summary implied), and search_code's ranking is an EXACT formula (in_degree + Function/Method:+10 + Route:+15 + vendored:-50 + test:-5), not a vague "rank by structural importance". Both required a real refactor after the fact, not a cosmetic tweak.
why: A worker mid-implementation has no way to know a more authoritative grounding doc is about to land -- but ANY worker resuming or re-verifying x06.P1-adjacent work must re-check the schemas doc's relevant section against the current implementation before trusting it, because earlier-generation docs (scout digests) are explicitly superseded in precision by later ground-truth extractions on the same tool.
howToApply: When implementing or reviewing parity-floor behavior (search_graph/get_graph_schema/search_code/get_code_snippet/etc.), always check x06-baseline-tool-schemas.md's per-tool section FIRST if it exists for that tool -- it is more authoritative than x06-source-scout-digests.md's summary-level claims, and it evolves as new sections get filled in (this session found it went from having ONLY tools 1-8 to also covering framing details for tools 9-16 across the session).

statement: During the fix pass, the orchestrator's zero-trust rerun caught an integration-test/implementation desync: graph_schema.rs's get_graph_schema() was correctly refactored to sort descending-by-count (per the baseline schemas doc), but tests/parity_read_tools.rs's own integration test still asserted the OLD alphabetical-ordering expectation from before that refactor -- a same-lane, same-session desync between an implementation change and a test file that should have been updated in the same edit but was not.
why: When a baseline-parity-driven refactor changes an OBSERVABLE ordering/behavior guarantee, every test asserting that guarantee -- not just the unit tests co-located with the implementation -- must be swept in the same change. The unit tests in graph_schema.rs itself were updated correctly; the separate integration-test file was missed because it lives in a different file the refactor didn't visually pass through.
howToApply: After any refactor that changes an ordering/ranking/format guarantee, grep the whole crate (src/ AND tests/) for assertions on that guarantee's shape (e.g. grep for the field name plus "sort"/"order"/"alphabetical") before considering the refactor done -- do not rely on `cargo test` catching it during normal iteration if the refactor and the test-run happen to be separated by other work in between (as happened here: the refactor landed in the first push, the desync was only caught by an INDEPENDENT verification pass, not by the worker's own pre-push test run, because integration tests were last run before the graph_schema.rs ordering refactor in this exact sequence).

statement: This session's worktree (agent-a13d841a23f84d9ab under C:\Projects\ocentra-enforcer\.claude\worktrees\) experienced severe, sustained cargo package-cache lock contention ("Blocking waiting for file lock on package cache") from many concurrent sibling-agent git/cargo processes sharing the same machine -- a cold cargo build --workspace took ~17-27 minutes even with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4, and background bash tasks were repeatedly killed by an apparent task-lifetime limit mid-compile, requiring re-launch-and-resume rather than a single long-running call. Additionally, an initial `git checkout -B <lane> origin/rust-build` timed out mid-operation and left a stale index.lock plus a half-checked-out working tree (files from two different branch lineages mixed together) that had to be diagnosed and cleanly reset before real work could start.
why: This is infrastructure-level flakiness, not a code defect -- any worker or orchestrator re-verifying this lane's gates from a fresh checkout on the same contended machine should expect multi-tens-of-minutes gate runs and budget accordingly, and should recognize a mid-command timeout during checkout/build as likely contention (check for a stale index.lock with a static mtime before assuming corruption).
howToApply: When a build/test/checkout command times out on this shared machine, check the background task's actual log tail before concluding it hung -- it is very likely still making real progress (observed repeatedly: warnings/Compiling lines kept appearing across many consecutive re-checks). Prefer re-running the SAME background command with a longer implicit wait (via Monitor or repeated log-tail checks) over killing and restarting from scratch, since incremental caching means a second attempt is much faster than the first cold one.
